plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: Pale pink-lilac goblets rise straight out of bare ground, with no leaves in sight. They look like crocuses and appear in damp meadows just as summer fades. The leaves come up the following spring, long after the flowers have gone.
plants.location: Damp meadows and open woodland across Europe, including the UK
plants.funFact: It is not a true crocus. It belongs to a different family, and every part of it contains colchicine, a powerful toxin. Colchicine is also used in plant breeding and in medicine.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: This is the largest protea. Its dinner-plate flower heads are crowned with silky, pink-tipped bracts around a central cluster of true flowers. It grows as a tough evergreen shrub on the fynbos slopes of the Cape. In late winter and spring the slopes are covered in these flowers.
plants.bloomingSeason: Mainly winter and spring, June to October (September is the Southern Hemisphere spring)
plants.location: Fynbos of the Western and Eastern Cape, South Africa
plants.funFact: It is South Africa's national flower. Fynbos plants like it have evolved to survive periodic wildfires, and it resprouts from a woody underground base.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.description: Whole trees turn into clouds of fluffy, honey-scented golden pompoms. Each ball is made up of dozens of tiny flowers. In the Australian bush it is a bright sign that spring has arrived.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late winter to spring, peaking from August to September
plants.location: Southeastern Australia, from South Australia and Victoria into New South Wales
plants.funFact: Golden wattle is Australia's national floral emblem. Its green and gold colors are also the country's official national colors.

plants.name: Symphyotrichum novae-angliae
plants.description: Tall, sturdy stems carry masses of violet-purple, daisy-like flowers with golden centers. They burst into color when most other meadow plants are fading. Migrating monarch butterflies and many native bees feed on them.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer to fall, roughly August to October
plants.location: Prairies, meadows and roadsides of eastern and central North America
plants.funFact: It is sometimes called Michaelmas daisy because it flowers around the feast of St. Michael on September 29.
